items.name: Pixar
clues: It makes things that take years to finish and about ninety minutes to enjoy.
It began as the computer graphics group of the film company behind Star Wars.
In 1986 a tech boss who had just been pushed out of his own company bought it for about ten million dollars.
After the deal, its own bosses were also put in charge of the buyer’s famous animation studio.
Disney bought it in 2006 for about 7.4 billion dollars, which made Steve Jobs Disney’s biggest single shareholder.
Its logo has a little jumping desk lamp, and its first feature film was Toy Story (1995).

items.name: WhatsApp
clues: You have probably used it today, possibly to complain about this class.
Two former Yahoo engineers started it in California in 2009.
One of the founders had once applied for a job at the company that later bought it, and been turned down.
Both founders left the buyer within about four years, and one of them later tweeted that it was time to delete the buyer’s main app.
Facebook paid about 19 billion dollars for it in 2014, when it had around 55 employees.
Its name is a pun on a casual way of saying hello, and its logo is a white phone in a green speech bubble.

items.name: YouTube
clues: People open it to watch one thing and end up, two hours later, somewhere completely different.
Three former employees of the online payment company PayPal started it in 2005.
The first thing anybody uploaded to it was 19 seconds long and filmed at a zoo in San Diego.
Many people thought the buyer had paid far too much for a company that made almost no money and was facing copyright complaints.
Google bought it for 1.65 billion dollars in shares in 2006, less than two years after it started.
Its logo is a red play button, and people who make a living on it are named after it.

items.name: Minecraft
clues: Millions of children have spent more time in it than in their own garden.
A Swedish programmer started it on his own in 2009, in his spare time.
It became so popular that its creator set up a small company in Stockholm to look after it.
When it was sold, its creator left and wrote online: “It’s not about the money. It’s about my sanity.”
In 2014 Microsoft bought the company behind it for 2.5 billion dollars.
Everything in it is made of blocks, there’s a green monster called a Creeper, and it’s the best-selling video game of all time.

items.name: Beats
clues: You’ve probably seen footballers wearing its products as they get off the team bus.
A rapper and a record company boss started it in the late 2000s because they thought most people heard music badly.
At first its products were made with a cable company called Monster, until the partners split.
After the deal, both founders went to work for the buyer, and its streaming service became the starting point for the buyer’s own music service.
Apple paid about 3 billion dollars for it in 2014, more than it had ever paid for a company.
Headphones with a red “b” logo, started by Dr. Dre.

items.name: Volvo
clues: Its customers are famous for caring more about safety than speed.
It started in Gothenburg, Sweden, in 1927, as part of a ball-bearing company.
In 1959 one of its engineers invented the modern three-point seatbelt, and the company let every carmaker use the design for free.
An American carmaker bought it in 1999 and sold it again about ten years later.
Since 2010 it has belonged to Geely, a Chinese car company, but it is still based in Sweden.
Its name is Latin for “I roll”, and its logo is a circle with an arrow.
